name: The dualism of life and matter (elan vital)
plain_explanation: Bergson pictures the universe as a struggle between two opposed forces: an upward-climbing life-force pushing to find new outlets, and a downward-falling matter that resists and partly channels it -- rather like a stream splitting around obstacles.
precise_definition: Bergson's central metaphysical dualism, unlike most historical systems, dividing reality into life (a single vital impulse, or elan vital, given once for all at the world's beginning, struggling to break through and organize matter) and matter (the inert 'downward' motion that resists and is used by life), evolution being the ongoing clash and adaptation between the two.
why_it_mattered: It is the foundation for Bergson's entire philosophy of creative, unpredictable evolution, and for his opposition to both mechanism and teleology as accounts of biological development.
historical_origin: Set out especially in Creative Evolution.
examples: Life as 'one vast vital impulse... divided by the obstacles it encounters into diverging currents, like the wind at the street-corner'
The universe compared to a cone, with movement up (life) and movement down (matter/becoming misapprehended by intellect)
The image of life as a shell bursting into fragments that are again shells
objections: Russell: much of this, considered as poetry rather than argument, 'is in the main not capable of either proof or disproof' -- 'if you like Bergson's image better, it is just as legitimate' than Shakespeare's or Shelley's
competing_positions: Mechanism, which regards the future as implicit in the past with no essential novelty
Teleology, which supposes a predetermined goal toward which evolution moves
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly inspired Sorel's use of Bergsonian irrationalism for revolutionary syndicalism and Shaw's Back to Methuselah.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Russell notes its main political effect was conservative, harmonizing with the outlook culminating in Vichy.
